summary: Clarifies how to handle the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) SignedData content type when more than one digital signature is present. It updates the CMS specification, RFC 3852, so implementations treat multiple signers consistently. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC clarifies how recipients process CMS signed content when it contains multiple signatures. Usually, one valid signature from a signer is enough to treat that signer as having signed the content.

questions: how does cms handle multiple signers
why use multiple signatures for the same content
how does cms handle multiple signatures from one signer
subtitle: Clarifying how CMS recipients process several signatures from one signer.

tldr.problem: RFC 3852 did not clearly explain how recipients should process SignedData when a signer provides more than one digital signature.
tldr.mechanism: The clarification says that one valid signature associated with a signer is usually treated as a successful signature by that signer; applications using another rule must specify it.
tldr.outcome: It makes the multiple-signature processing rule clearer and updates RFC 3852.

today: RFC 4853 updates RFC 3852 with a clarification for multiple signatures. The memo is Standards Track.

sections.title: The Multiple-Signature Question
sections.content:
Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) SignedData allows multiple digital signatures, but RFC 3852 did not clearly state how a recipient should process them. RFC 4853 replaces some text in RFC 3852 to clarify the rule for signatures associated with a given signer.

Multiple signatures can help recipients who support different algorithms or who are moving from one algorithm to another. The RFC gives RSA and ECDSA as examples of different algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS can carry more than one signature on signed content. This RFC explains how recipients should decide whether a signer successfully signed it.

sections.title: How a Recipient Treats Signatures
sections.content:
When more than one signature is present for a given signer, successful validation of one signature is usually treated as successful signing by that signer. An application that uses a different rule must specify that rule. If matching signer identifiers is not enough to tell which signatures came from the same signer, the application specification must describe how to make that decision.

Implementations MUST gracefully handle SignerInfo versions and signature algorithms they do not implement, as stated in the updated text.
sections.plainLanguage: A recipient usually needs to validate only one signature from a signer. An application that requires a different result must state its rule clearly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the replacement text should reduce the likelihood of interoperability errors during transitions from MD5 and SHA-1 to stronger one-way hash functions or better signature algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: The clarification is intended to reduce disagreements between implementations during algorithm transitions.

sections.title: Status of the Clarification
sections.content: RFC 4853 updates RFC 3852. Its status is Standards Track, as stated in the memo. The clarification changes processing rules for multiple signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: This Standards Track document updates the CMS text in RFC 3852.
